name: Health and Culture week at AKU-SONAM EA

content.title: Health and Culture week at AKU-SONAM EA
content.summary: Nursing and Midwifery students host health and culture week to learn how to provide open-minded and culturally-sensitive care

media.caption: Mr Samwel Gatimu (extreme right in grey shirt) poses for a picture with students during the potluck
media.alt: Health and Culture week at AKU-SONAM EA

content.text: "The importance of having culture as part of their training is to equip them with the skills to be able to offer nursing care that is culturally competent, gender-sensitive and holistic" says Samwel Gatimu, the supervising instructor who curated the Health and Culture week at the Aga Khan University School of Nursing and Midwifery (AKU-SONAM) in Kenya.

On October 2, 2019, students from the Bachelor of Science in Midwifery and Nursing (BScM and BScN) at AKU-SONAM prepared a potluck for fellow students and staff to relish. This was organized as part of the Health and Culture week* celebrated by students annually to recognize the different tribes and cultures that exemplify Kenya. On September 26, they visited the Bomas of Kenya to view the traditional homes, familiarize themselves with the tribes represented in Kenya and enjoyed the traditional dance presentations.

According to Mr Gatimu, the potluck was key to appreciating the nuances inherent in each community, especially in reference to food. He shares, "We wanted the students to find out how the meals that different communities partake in affect people's health. Which meals do some communities take that improve their health but are not taken by other communities? How do cultural differences affect the provision of care? These are some of the things we wanted them to learn."

To drive the point home, Mr Gatimu recalled a time during his midwifery practice when cultural aspects influenced his service provision. "In some Cushitic communities, women expect to be handled only by another woman during delivery, yet I was the midwife available. I had to talk to the patient and her family until they appreciated that they were better off with me providing care rather than have them go without care. Ultimately, I handled the delivery."

Many students, including Dorcas Kyove and Gladys Makena in the BScN programme, appreciated the relevance of these lessons as part of the curriculum. Ms Kyove shared that her visit to Bomas illuminated the reality of polygamy in some African communities. She went ahead to reveal that "We nurse patients who have been abused, and sometimes we can become judgmental as nurses, but culturally we should accept patients as they are without judging them and be open-minded." Ms Makena expressed similar sentiments, saying that "In most cultures, men had their own huts as the head of the family. In nursing, I've dealt with women who have to consult their husbands on many issues including family planning, pregnancy, and general health decisions to know if the husband is alright with the decisions they're about to make. I have to respect that culture and be open-minded because cultures are different and always changing."
* AKU-SONAM hosts a Health and Culture week annually to promote the celebration of cultural diversity with a specific focus on how culture impacts health.
